innate.name: Making functional things from what you absorb
innate.behavior: You sit through a two-hour workshop on a new framework, and by the end of the day you have a working prototype deployed. Your colleagues are still reading the setup guide; you are already showing them a URL. When someone describes a workflow problem, you do not write a requirements document — you sketch three variations in a notebook, pick one, and start building. The output is not polished marketing material; it is a tool that runs, a process that completes, a clear explanation that removes confusion. You do not announce the work in advance or wait for approval — the thing appears, and then people use it. Your energy rises while you work this way because each finished piece proves to you that you understand the subject. The validation comes from the artifact itself, not from someone else's praise.
innate.evidence: Eating God is the heaviest force in the structure, sitting at 9. Metal appears as the month stem Xin (Eating God to Ji earth day master), hidden as Xin inside the day branch You, and again in the hidden stems of both the month and hour Si branches — each contribution adding to the total. Metal sits on the list of favorable elements (metal, water, wood), meaning the structure needs you to use this output channel. The day master Ji earth is slightly strong, supported by fire Resource in the two Si branches and reinforced by earth across three pillars; using metal output drains the excess and brings the system into balance. When an ability both matches your heaviest Ten God and appears on the favorable list, it recharges you while you use it.

trained.name: Absorbing structured knowledge as a buffer before acting
trained.behavior: Before launching anything, you enroll in one more course, read one more manual, earn one more certification. You treat formal learning as a necessary precondition for legitimacy. When someone asks you to lead a project in an adjacent domain, your first instinct is not 'I can figure it out as I go' but 'I should study it properly first.' You respect teachers, institutions, and documented processes; you trust that following the established method will keep you safe. This pattern was useful early on — it gave you real skills and built a foundation. But over time it becomes a delay tactic. You accumulate credentials that no one asked for, and the absorption phase stretches longer than the doing phase. The cost is that you know more than you show, and opportunities close before you finish preparing.
trained.trained_by: Wood appears in the year pillar as Yi, acting as Seven Killings — a pressure or constraint present from early life. Seven Killings sitting at 5 suggests moderate but persistent external demand or criticism, the kind that teaches you to meet a standard before stepping forward. At the same time, Wealth is nearly absent: Indirect Wealth registers only 1 (one Gui water hidden in the year branch Chou), Direct Wealth is completely missing (0), and water as an element does not appear at all in the eight visible characters. The gap between making things (Eating God at 9) and earning recognition or money (Wealth at nearly zero) created an early belief: 'My work is not enough by itself; I need formal backing to make it count.' Direct Resource, representing systems and credentials, sits at 6 — Bing fire hidden in both the month and hour Si branches, feeding the day master. That weight is moderate but present, and you learned to rely on it as proof of readiness rather than as one input among many.
trained.evidence: Direct Resource weight is 6. Fire appears twice as Bing hidden in the month branch Si and the hour branch Si, both acting as Direct Resource to the Ji earth day master. Fire as an element registers 2 across the chart. The structure says the useful gods are metal, water, and wood — fire (Resource family) is not on that list, meaning the chart does not need more of it. Yet you keep returning to it because the early environment (Seven Killings pressure in the year, Wealth absence across the board) taught you that preparation is safer than exposure.

defensive.name: Relying on your own judgment and peer circles as the final measure of quality
defensive.behavior: When you finish a project, you do not pitch it to a buyer or ship it to a broad audience — you show it to two or three people whose taste you trust, and their nod is enough. You form tight working relationships with people who think like you, and inside that circle you feel confident. You hold strong opinions about how things should be built, and you would rather walk away from a deal than compromise the design. To outsiders this reads as independence or integrity. But the underlying mechanism is defensive: you are using peer validation and personal standards as a substitute for market validation. You built this reflex because early on, the market did not respond proportionally to your effort — you made things, and they did not sell or get promoted the way you expected. So you shifted the goalpost inward. Now the work is 'done' when you and your circle say it is, not when it generates income or formal recognition. The cost is that you stay small. You keep your best work inside communities that already agree with you, and you do not test it in the wider environment where money and leverage actually move.
defensive.looks_like: Independence, strong personal judgment, loyalty to peers, unwillingness to compromise on craft
defensive.actual_cost: You substitute peer approval for market feedback, which keeps you in the maker role rather than moving you toward seller, owner, or leader roles. Your income ceiling stays low because you end projects at 'my friends think it is good' rather than 'it sold' or 'it earned me a position.' You dismiss opportunities that require you to adapt your output to someone else's requirements, labeling them as 'selling out,' but the real issue is that you never built comfort with the Wealth-to-Officer translation — turning output into money, and money into formal standing. The structure shows this gap clearly: Wealth is nearly absent, and the first luck pillar that brings sustained water (Wealth family) does not arrive until age 42.
defensive.evidence: Companion sits at 8, second only to Eating God. The day stem is Ji earth, the hour stem is also Ji earth (both acting as Companion to the day master), the year branch Chou hides Ji earth, and the two Si branches each hide Wu earth (Rob Wealth, part of the Companion family, contributing 2 total). Earth as an element registers 3 across the chart. But the day master is already labeled slightly strong (偏旺), meaning the structure has too much earth and does not need more reinforcement. The list of favorable elements is metal, water, and wood — earth is not on it. When a Ten God is heavy but not favorable, it usually signals a compensatory pattern: you rely on it not because it balances you, but because other pathways are blocked. The block here is Wealth: Indirect Wealth is 1, Direct Wealth is 0, and water is completely missing from the visible pillars. Without a natural bridge from Output to Income, you learned to close the loop internally — you and your peers decide the work is good, and that becomes the reward.

one_leverage: Keep the ability to make functional things from what you absorb (Eating God at 9). It is the only ability that both recharges you while you use it and sits on the list of elements the structure needs. The other two patterns — absorbing credentials and relying on peer validation — were trained into you by early conditions (pressure without proportional reward), and they drain your energy even when they look like strengths. If you strip everything else away and trust only this one lever, you will still produce work that proves your competence, and that proof will eventually draw the resources and recognition the structure currently lacks. The gap in Wealth starts to fill at age 42 when the Bing Zi luck pillar brings water onto the branch, and it deepens at age 52 when Yi Hai brings both water and wood. Between now and then, let the work itself be the negotiation — ship it, show it, price it — and stop treating peer approval or one more certification as the condition for going public. The structure is already built for output; the only thing missing is the willingness to let that output enter the market.
